The periodontitis-decreased genera reach the top 5% or pass FDR in no dataset.

## Head and neck cancer and smoking

Head and neck cancer and smoking are the conditions whose genera are most often reported in the same directions as periodontitis (see the direction summary above). With 15–16 studies each, no taxon reaches even unadjusted p < 0.05 in a binomial test. These heatmaps therefore use descriptive taxon sets chosen by a relaxed rule, which are not equivalent to the consensus signatures.

```{r bsdb-hnc-heatmap}

The PerioSigDB consensus comes from a binomial test of increased vs decreased signatures, unadjusted p < 0.05. Row colour: red, increased in periodontitis; blue, decreased. Brackets: PerioSigDB signatures (rows) or head and neck cancer studies (columns) reporting the taxon increased / decreased. The top-left and bottom-right blocks are the same direction as periodontitis. Rows are ordered by NCBI taxonomic lineage within each direction. Red means more like increased and blue more like decreased, with full colour at a difference of 0.7 or more. Columns are grouped by family. Families are ordered by their mean difference, and taxa within a family by their own. The order runs red to blue for head and neck cancer's increased taxa and blue to red for its decreased taxa."

Both conditions match periodontitis mainly through the decreased taxa: *Haemophilus*, *Neisseria*, *Rothia* and *Corynebacterium* in head and neck cancer, and *Haemophilus*, *Neisseria*, *Corynebacterium* and *Granulicatella* in smoking. Their increased taxa match less consistently, and some go the opposite way (*Porphyromonas* in head and neck cancer; *Peptostreptococcus* and *Selenomonas* in smoking).

# Do the periodontitis-associated genera co-vary in health?

Periodontitis studies report some genera increased together (e.g. *Treponema* and *Tannerella*) and others decreased together. Is that grouping particular to disease, or do these genera already co-vary in healthy mouths? The BugSigDB paper asked this for stool and found the second: genera reported together in disease signatures mostly mirror how they co-occur in healthy stool (Geistlinger et al. 2024, Figure 4). Healthy subgingival plaque from the Human Microbiome Project (HMP; one first-visit sample from each of 183 participants) answers the same question for the periodontitis-associated genera.

A positive correlation between two genera means that, across healthy participants, both tend to be abundant in the same plaque samples. A negative correlation means that where one is abundant, the other tends to be scarce. Relative abundances sum to one, so a genus taking a larger share lowers the share of every other genus. That creates correlations that need not reflect how the genera's amounts vary (Friedman and Alm 2012). The correlations therefore use centred log-ratio (CLR) abundance, each genus relative to the geometric mean of all genera in the same sample, which removes most of this effect. Even so, a correlation need not mean a direct ecological interaction. The five PerioSigDB 16S studies with per-sample data give the same correlations in their healthy participants and, separately, in their periodontitis patients.

```{r co-occurrence-hmp}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 3.6
#| fig-align: left
#| fig-cap: "Correlation between pairs of the periodontitis-associated genera in healthy subgingival plaque from the Human Microbiome Project. There are 183 participants, first visit only, so one sample each. Genera: the periodontitis-associated genera with at least 0.1% relative abundance in at least 10% of samples. That leaves 12 of the 19 periodontitis-increased and 11 of the 12 periodontitis-decreased genera. Each point is a pair of genera: the Spearman correlation of their CLR abundance. CLR abundance is the log of the genus relative to the geometric mean of all genera in the sample. Rows: whether both genera are increased (66 pairs), both decreased (55) or one of each (132) in periodontitis. Bar and number: median. p: is the row's median higher (both increased, both decreased) or lower (one of each) than for random pairs of these genera? The one-sided permutation test shuffles which genera count as increased and which as decreased (1,000 permutations), because pairs share genera. Faded: p ≥ 0.05. The next figure repeats this in the five PerioSigDB studies with per-sample data."
# subgingival plaque samples of healthy and untreated periodontitis participants in the PerioSigDB studies with
# deposited reads and participant annotations (scripts/participant_data_1-download.R and participant_data_2-dada2.R)
participant_samples <- read.csv("../../output/participant_data/sample_metadata.csv") |>
  filter(site == "subgingival plaque", status %in% c("healthy", "periodontitis")) |>
  mutate(group = ifelse(status == "healthy", "Health", "Periodontitis"))

hmp_cor <- readRDS("../../output/hmp_subgingival_correlation.rds")

perio_dir <- setNames(perio_genera$direction, perio_genera$taxon)
in_hmp <- intersect(perio_genera$taxon, rownames(hmp_cor))
pair_cor <- as_tibble(as.table(hmp_cor[in_hmp, in_hmp]), .name_repair = "minimal") |>
  setNames(c("a", "b", "healthy")) |>
  mutate(across(c(a, b), as.character)) |>
  filter(a < b) |>
  mutate(pair = case_when(perio_dir[a] != perio_dir[b] ~ "One increased,\none decreased",
                          perio_dir[a] == "increased" ~ "Both increased", .default = "Both decreased"))
# is each kind of pair more (two increased, two decreased) or less (one of each) correlated than random pairs
# of the same genera? One test per kind of pair, of its median correlation; pairs share genera, so instead of
# a test over pairs, the genera's directions in periodontitis are permuted (the same 1,000 permutations for
# every test), which keeps 12 increased and 11 decreased genera; one-sided p
pair_types <- c("Both increased", "Both decreased", "One increased,\none decreased")
pair_side <- c(1, 1, -1)
pair_kind <- \(dir, a, b) ifelse(dir[a] != dir[b], pair_types[3], ifelse(dir[a] == "increased", pair_types[1], pair_types[2]))
pair_medians <- \(d, dir) tapply(d$r, factor(pair_kind(dir, d$a, d$b), levels = pair_types), median)
set.seed(1)
perms <- replicate(1000, setNames(sample(perio_dir[in_hmp]), in_hmp), simplify = FALSE)
type_test <- \(d) {
  obs <- pair_medians(d, perio_dir)
  null <- sapply(perms, \(dir) pair_medians(d, dir))
  tibble(pair = pair_types, median = as.vector(obs), all_pairs = median(d$r),
         null_lo = apply(null, 1, quantile, 0.025), null_hi = apply(null, 1, quantile, 0.975),
         p = map_dbl(seq_along(pair_types), \(i) (1 + sum(pair_side[i] * null[i, ] >= pair_side[i] * obs[i])) /
                                                  (1 + length(perms))))
}

# genus relative abundance per participant (mean of their subgingival samples) in the five studies with
# participant data
participant_genera <- read.csv("../../output/participant_data/taxon_abundance.csv") |>
  filter(rank == "genus") |>
  # HMP uses the former name of Cutibacterium
  mutate(taxon = ifelse(taxon == "Cutibacterium", "Propionibacterium", taxon)) |>
  filter(taxon %in% in_hmp) |>
  inner_join(participant_samples, by = c("Study", "run_accession")) |>
  summarise(abundance = mean(relative_abundance), .by = c(Study, subject, group, taxon))

# centred log-ratio (CLR) abundance, as for HMP, so that the shares summing to one do not create
# correlations: over each participant's full genus profile, zeros replaced by half the participant's
# smallest non-zero abundance
participant_clr <- read.csv("../../output/participant_data/taxon_abundance.csv") |>
  filter(rank == "genus") |>
  mutate(taxon = ifelse(taxon == "Cutibacterium", "Propionibacterium", taxon)) |>
  inner_join(participant_samples, by = c("Study", "run_accession")) |>
  summarise(abundance = mean(relative_abundance), .by = c(Study, subject, group, taxon)) |>
  filter(any(abundance > 0), .by = c(Study, taxon)) |>
  mutate(x = ifelse(abundance > 0, abundance, min(abundance[abundance > 0]) / 2),
         clr = log(x) - mean(log(x)), .by = c(Study, subject)) |>
  # a genus never detected in a study's group gives no correlation there
  semi_join(filter(participant_genera, abundance > 0), by = c("Study", "group", "taxon")) |>
  select(Study, subject, group, taxon, clr)

# Spearman correlation of each pair within each study; a genus never detected in a study's participants
# gives no correlation there
study_cor <- function(g, d = participant_clr, v = "clr") {
  d |>
    filter(group == g) |>
    select(Study, subject, group, taxon, all_of(v)) |>
    pivot_wider(names_from = taxon, values_from = all_of(v)) |>
    nest(.by = Study) |>
    mutate(n = map_int(data, nrow),
           r = map(data, \(d) suppressWarnings(cor(select(d, -subject, -group), method = "spearman")))) |>
    mutate(r = map(r, \(m) as_tibble(as.table(m), .name_repair = "minimal") |> setNames(c("a", "b", "r")))) |>
    select(Study, n, r) |>
    unnest(r) |>
    mutate(across(c(a, b), as.character)) |>
    filter(a < b, !is.na(r))
}
# one column for HMP and one for each study (correlations within that study), health in the top row and
# periodontitis in the bottom row, pair types within each panel
hmp_samples <- readRDS("../../output/hmp_oral_prevalence.rds") |>
  filter(site == "Subgingival Plaque") |>
  pull(samples) |>
  first()
study_n <- distinct(participant_clr, Study, subject, group) |>
  count(Study, group) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = group, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(column = sprintf("%s\n(%d healthy, %d periodontitis)", Study, Health, Periodontitis))
columns <- c(sprintf("HMP\n(%d healthy)", hmp_samples), study_n$column)
cooc_plot <- bind_rows(
  transmute(pair_cor, a, b, r = healthy, group = "Health", column = columns[1]),
  map(c("Health", "Periodontitis"), \(g) transmute(study_cor(g), Study, a, b, r, group = g)) |>
    bind_rows() |>
    inner_join(select(study_n, Study, column), by = "Study") |>
    select(-Study)
) |>
  inner_join(select(pair_cor, a, b, pair), by = c("a", "b")) |>
  mutate(column = factor(column, levels = columns), pair = factor(pair, levels = rev(pair_types)),
         group = factor(group, levels = c("Health", "Periodontitis")))
# the three tests within each panel (HMP, and each study and group; unadjusted p); a row is faded when its
# test is not significant
cooc_tests <- cooc_plot |>
  nest(.by = c(column, group)) |>
  mutate(tests = map(data, type_test)) |>
  select(-data) |>
  unnest(tests)
row_significant <- cooc_tests |>
  select(column, group, pair, p) |>
  mutate(pair = factor(pair, levels = levels(cooc_plot$pair)), significant = p < 0.05)
cooc_plot <- left_join(cooc_plot, select(row_significant, -p), by = c("column", "group", "pair"))
cooc_median <- summarise(cooc_plot, r = median(r), .by = c(column, pair, group, significant))
row_p <- row_significant
# studies (not HMP) where a kind of pair differs from random pairs at p < 0.05, for the text
n_sig <- \(g, pt) sum(cooc_tests$p[cooc_tests$group == g & cooc_tests$pair == pt & cooc_tests$column != columns[1]] < 0.05)
n_word <- \(n) if (n == 0) "none" else as.character(n)

# one panel per column (HMP and each study) and group; cols selects the columns shown
cooc_figure <- function(cols, title) {
    ggplot(filter(cooc_plot, column %in% cols), aes(r, pair)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
    geom_quasirandom(aes(fill = pair, alpha = significant, color = significant), orientation = "y", width = 0.3,
                     shape = 21, size = 1.3, stroke = 0.2) +
    geom_crossbar(data = filter(cooc_median, column %in% cols), aes(xmin = r, xmax = r, color = significant), width = 0.65, linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_label(data = filter(cooc_median, column %in% cols), aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", ifelse(abs(r) < 0.005, 0, r)), color = significant),
               nudge_y = 0.42, size = 2.7, fill = "white", border.colour = NA, label.padding = unit(0.1, "lines")) +
    geom_text(data = filter(row_p, column %in% cols), aes(x = -Inf, label = sprintf("p = %s", signif(p, 1)), color = significant),
              hjust = -0.08, nudge_y = 0.42, size = 2.6, fontface = "italic") +
    scale_alpha_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = 0.75, `FALSE` = 0.2), guide = "none") +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "grey10", `FALSE` = "grey65"), guide = "none") +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c("Both increased" = "#c2410c", "Both decreased" = "#1c5cab",
                                 "One increased,\none decreased" = "grey75"), guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(-0.5, 0, 0.5)) +
    facet_grid(group ~ column, switch = "y") +
    labs(x = "Correlation of the pair across participants (Spearman, CLR abundance)", y = NULL,
         title = title) +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 10), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
          strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, hjust = 1), strip.placement = "outside")
}

cooc_figure(columns[1], NULL) + theme(strip.text.y.left = element_blank()) +
  labs(x = "Correlation of the pair across participants\n(Spearman, CLR abundance)")
```

In healthy plaque, genera that change the same way in periodontitis also rise and fall together. Decreased pairs (median 0.35) and increased pairs (0.18) correlate more than random pairs of these genera, and opposite pairs less (−0.23). Some disease-associated groupings therefore already exist in healthy variation, although cross-sectional samples cannot show a path to disease.

```{r co-occurrence}
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 7.4
#| fig-cap: "Correlation between pairs of the 23 genera of the figure above, within each group of participants. These are the 12 periodontitis-increased and 11 periodontitis-decreased genera that pass the abundance filter. Left column: healthy subgingival plaque from the Human Microbiome Project (first visit only, so one sample per participant). Other columns: the five PerioSigDB studies with per-sample data. Healthy participants are in the top row and periodontitis patients in the bottom row. Each point is a pair of genera: the Spearman correlation of their CLR abundance across the participants of that study and group. CLR abundance is the log of the genus relative to the geometric mean of all genera in the sample. Each participant gives one value, the mean of their subgingival samples. Rows within each panel: whether both genera are increased (66 pairs), both decreased (55) or one of each (132) in periodontitis. Bar and number: median. p: is the row's median higher (both increased, both decreased) or lower (one of each) than for random pairs of these genera? The one-sided permutation test shuffles which genera count as increased and which as decreased (1,000 permutations), because pairs share genera. Each panel is tested on its own (unadjusted). Faded: p ≥ 0.05."
cooc_figure(columns, NULL)
```

In the healthy participants of the five studies, decreased pairs correlate more than random pairs in `r n_sig("Health", pair_types[2])` studies and increased pairs in `r n_sig("Health", pair_types[1])`. In their periodontitis patients, decreased pairs still do in `r n_sig("Periodontitis", pair_types[2])` studies and increased pairs in `r n_word(n_sig("Periodontitis", pair_types[1]))`. In disease the decreased genera keep co-varying, while the increased genera no longer stand out from random pairs.

# Where do these genera live in the healthy mouth?

The Human Microbiome Project sampled nine sites in the mouths of the same healthy people. The figure shows at which of these sites each periodontitis-associated genus lives in health, for both the increased and the decreased genera.

```{r oral-habitat}
#| fig-width: 16
#| fig-height: 9.5
#| fig-cap: "Prevalence (A) and mean relative abundance (B) of the periodontitis-associated genera across the nine oral sites of the Human Microbiome Project. Samples come from healthy participants at their first visit (16S V3–V5). A: share of samples from that site with the genus at 0.1% relative abundance or more. B: the genus's share of reads, averaged over the site's samples, in percent (label). Colour in B is scaled within each genus on a log scale, relative to its highest site. It shows where each genus peaks rather than how genera compare in abundance. Rows: the periodontitis-associated genera present in HMP under the same name. Within each direction they are ordered by prevalence in subgingival plaque minus mean prevalence at the seven non-plaque sites, plaque-associated at top. Both panels have the same rows. Genera at 0% prevalence at five or more sites are left out. Columns: sites with their number of samples. They are grouped by the three oral community types of Segata et al. 2012: plaque; buccal mucosa, gingiva and palate; and tongue, saliva, tonsils and throat."
# precomputed by scripts/hmp_oral_prevalence.R (all nine oral sites)
# sites grouped into the three community types of Segata et al. 2012 (same HMP samples)
site_levels <- c("Subgingival Plaque", "Supragingival Plaque", "Buccal Mucosa", "Attached Keratinized Gingiva",
                 "Hard Palate", "Tongue Dorsum", "Saliva", "Palatine Tonsils", "Throat")
site_labels <- c("Sub-\ngingival\nplaque", "Supra-\ngingival\nplaque", "Buccal\nmucosa", "Attached\ngingiva",
                 "Hard\npalate", "Tongue\ndorsum", "Saliva", "Palatine\ntonsils", "Throat")
site_groups <- setNames(rep(c("Plaque", "Buccal mucosa, gingiva, palate", "Tongue, saliva, tonsils, throat"),
                            c(2, 3, 4)), site_levels)
hmp_sites <- readRDS("../../output/hmp_oral_prevalence.rds")
site_n <- distinct(hmp_sites, site, samples)

oral_habitat <- perio_genera |>
  select(taxon, direction) |>
  inner_join(select(hmp_sites, site, taxon, prevalence = prevalence_01, abundance = mean_abundance), by = "taxon") |>
  mutate(plaque_bias = prevalence[site == "Subgingival Plaque"] -
           mean(prevalence[!site %in% c("Subgingival Plaque", "Supragingival Plaque")]),
         .by = taxon)
# genera at 0% prevalence (rounded) at five or more of the nine sites are left out of the figure
habitat_rare <- oral_habitat |>
  summarise(zero_sites = sum(round(100 * prevalence) == 0), .by = taxon) |>
  filter(zero_sites >= 5) |>
  pull(taxon)

habitat_plot <- oral_habitat |>
  filter(!taxon %in% habitat_rare) |>
  mutate(habitat = factor(site_groups[site], levels = unique(site_groups)),
         site = factor(site, levels = site_levels,
                       labels = paste0(site_labels, "\n(", site_n$samples[match(site_levels, site_n$site)], ")")),
         direction = factor(direction, levels = c("increased", "decreased"),
                            labels = c("Increased in\nperiodontitis", "Decreased in\nperiodontitis")),
         taxon = fct_reorder(taxon, plaque_bias))

# abundance labels in percent of reads, with fewer decimals for larger values
pct_label <- \(a) {
  p <- 100 * a
  case_when(p == 0 ~ "0", p < 0.01 ~ "<0.01", p < 1 ~ sprintf("%.2f", p),
            p < 10 ~ sprintf("%.1f", p), TRUE ~ sprintf("%.0f", p))
}
# one heatmap; d has columns value (fill), label and dark (white text)
habitat_panel <- function(d, fill_scale) {
  ggplot(d, aes(site, taxon)) +
    geom_tile(aes(fill = value), color = "white", linewidth = 0.6) +
    geom_text(aes(label = label, color = dark), size = 2.7) +
    scale_color_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = "white", `FALSE` = "grey20"), guide = "none") +
    fill_scale +
    scale_x_discrete(position = "top") +
    guides(fill = guide_colourbar(title.position = "top", title.hjust = 0.5)) +
    facet_grid(direction ~ habitat, scales = "free", space = "free", switch = "y") +
    labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
    theme(axis.text.y = element_text(face = "italic"), strip.placement = "outside",
          strip.text.y.left = element_text(angle = 0, face = "bold"), strip.text.x = element_text(face = "bold"),
          panel.grid = element_blank(), panel.spacing.x = unit(0.25, "cm"),
          legend.position = "top", legend.title = element_text(size = 9), legend.key.width = unit(1.2, "cm"))
}
prev_panel <- habitat_panel(
  mutate(habitat_plot, value = prevalence, label = round(100 * prevalence), dark = prevalence > 0.55),
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7f7f7", high = "#08306b", labels = scales::percent, limits = c(0, 1),
                      name = "Prevalence (≥ 0.1% of reads)")
)
abund_panel <- habitat_panel(
  # colour scaled within each genus: log10 of abundance relative to the genus's highest site, floored at 1/100
  habitat_plot |>
    mutate(value = pmax(log10(abundance / max(abundance)), -2), .by = taxon) |>
    mutate(label = pct_label(abundance), dark = value > -0.75),
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#f7f7f7", high = "#08306b", limits = c(-2, 0), breaks = c(-2, -1, 0),
                      labels = c("≤ 1/100", "1/10", "Highest site"),
                      name = "Mean relative abundance,\nrelative to the genus's highest site")
) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank(), strip.text.y.left = element_blank())

# values quoted in the text: prevalence, and mean relative abundance in percent of reads
hp <- \(g, s) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * with(oral_habitat, prevalence[taxon == g & site == s]))
ha <- \(g, s) paste0(pct_label(with(oral_habitat, abundance[taxon == g & site == s])), "%")
ha_range <- \(g, sites) with(filter(oral_habitat, taxon == g, site %in% sites),
                             paste0(pct_label(min(abundance)), "–", pct_label(max(abundance)), "%"))
soft <- c("Attached Keratinized Gingiva", "Buccal Mucosa", "Hard Palate")

prev_panel + abund_panel + plot_annotation(tag_levels = "A")
```

Most periodontitis-decreased genera fall into two groups. *Streptococcus*, *Haemophilus* and *Gemella* are common throughout the mouth and most abundant on the soft tissues. *Streptococcus*, for example, makes up `r ha_range("Streptococcus", soft)` of reads on the gingiva, cheek and palate but `r ha("Streptococcus", "Subgingival Plaque")` in subgingival plaque. *Corynebacterium*, *Kingella* and *Cardiobacterium* live mainly in plaque: *Corynebacterium* is in `r hp("Corynebacterium", "Subgingival Plaque")` of subgingival plaque samples but only `r hp("Corynebacterium", "Tongue Dorsum")` of tongue samples.

The periodontitis-increased genera vary more. *Porphyromonas*, *Prevotella* and *Fusobacterium* occur in most samples at every site. *Treponema* and *Tannerella* are most common below the gumline: *Treponema* is in `r hp("Treponema", "Subgingival Plaque")` of subgingival samples and `r hp("Treponema", "Supragingival Plaque")` of supragingival ones. *Peptostreptococcus* is the exception, more common on the tongue (`r hp("Peptostreptococcus", "Tongue Dorsum")`) than in subgingival plaque (`r hp("Peptostreptococcus", "Subgingival Plaque")`). These healthy people were sampled once, so the data show where genera live, not where periodontitis taxa come from.
